newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bad news keeps coming in as Waigel fights for EMU.
newsitem.headline: Bad news keeps coming in as Waigel fights for EMU.

text.p: The bad news kept coming in for Theo Waigel on Thursday as Germany's finance minister vowed to do all to qualify for Europe's monetary union despite new data showing slower growth and stubbornly high unemployment.

Official figures showed year-on-year growth slowed in the first quarter of 1997 to 1.4 percent from 1.9 percent in the final 1996 quarter, making it hard for Bonn to reach its overall target of 2.5 percent growth for the full year.
Figures due out on Friday will indicate that the jobless total, not adjusted for seasonal variations, fell in May but still stood at 4.256 million after 4.347 million in April, official sources said.
The Federal Labour Office said it might need more funds to pay benefits.
After his humbling retreat from a grab for the Bundesbank's gold, analysts saw few solutions to Waigel's dilemma of plugging a 19 billion mark ($11 billion) budget gap.
This has to be filled to meet the three percent deficit-to-gross domestic product target to qualify for a single euro currency.

The once-taboo issue of delaying economic and monetary union (EMU) has started to appear in public discussion, prompting Waigel to warn against even considering missing the 1999 deadline for the euro.

"Germany will do everything to meet the criteria," he told a meeting of city government officials in Hamburg. "We are in the middle of the year that will decide currency union. So talk of a delay would be wrong."
The usually cheery Bavarian was downbeat when talking to journalists about the overall picture for Germany.
"The latest indicators are more positive but unfortunately they are not yet impacting on the labour market," he said.
The Federal Labour Office also saw little hope of change on the jobs front, where postwar record unemployment levels were expected to continue.

Office President Bernhard Jagoda said he might need almost seven billion marks in additional funds this year because he has to pay unemployment benefits for up to 4.2 million this year rather than 3.95 million as foreseen in his 1997 budget.
Waigel said that privatisation, an option analysts said was growing as the prospect of higher taxes seems to fade, "will be continued or may even be stepped up".

He hinted that sales of Bonn's shares in the postal bank Postbank, highway rest stops and the telecoms group Deutsche Telekom could bring in more revenue while a spending freeze should hold down expenditure. But he gave few details.

Pressed by journalists to explain the ceasefire he and Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer worked out on Tuesday, leading to his retreat from the gold grab, Waigel said only that their talks were constructive.
"We are having talks with the Bundesbank and only after that can a decision be reached on a change to the Bundesbank law," Waigel said.
"In public, the finance minister talks of still getting the budget into shape but the fact is he simply cannot make it," said economist Holger Fahrinkrug at UBS in Frankfurt.
Economists say Bonn should be able to find only four billion marks or so with the spending freeze and one-off moves like selling excess oil reserves.

While Waigel kept up the search for more money to meet the Maastricht treaty challenge, an opinion poll said 71 percent of German voters wanted EMU delayed and only 21 percent thought it should go ahead on time. Only 37 percent thought Germany could meet the criteria, while 45 percent did not.
The German press was scathing in its commentaries after Waigel, with much help from Kohl, survived a censure motion brought in parliament on Wednesday by the opposition.
"The coalition survived the parliament debate. But it is by no means over the hump," wrote the Frankfurter Allgemeine.
The Handelsblatt business daily, which said on Tuesday the only option left was for Waigel to resign, said responsibility for the budget mess should be spread a bit wider.
"The whole government is guilty of the fact it continues to stand on shaky ground," it wrote, describing the crisis as the most serious yet in Kohl's 15 years as chancellor. ($ = 1.728 German Marks)
